To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nearly all T cell clones have memory cell potential and that the composition of clonal memory populations matches the effector cell population generated early in the immune responses.
nearly all microbe-specific naive CD4+ T lymphocytes produce memory cells during an immune response.

1) Nearly all microbe-specific T cells that respond to infection become memory cells, 2) Memory cell potential is not limited to the most dominant T cell clones, and 3) Memory T cell populations are not homogeneous, as different clonal populations produce different ratios of effector cell populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the immune system responds to and remembers infections.
the mechanisms by which the immune system remembers past infections and protects the host from subsequent infection.
understanding how T cells are activated during infection.

nearly all T cells have the potential to give memory cells.
all naïve CD4 T cells have the potential to become memory cells.

nearly all T cell clones have the potential to give memory T cells and that memory T cells are a heterogeneous population of cells with distinct functions.

nearly every immunological T lymphocyte has the potential to become a memory T cell, which is important to consider when developing vaccines and immunotherapies.
